questions.question: Which of the following is the defining characteristic of a luminous object?
options: It reflects light from other sources very well.
It gives out its own light.
It lets light pass directly through it.
It absorbs all light that falls on it.

questions.question: How does the reflection of light from a mirror-like surface differ from that of a rough brick wall?
options: Only the mirror-like surface reflects light, while the brick wall absorbs all light.
The mirror-like surface reflects light in a regular way, whereas the brick wall scatters light.
The mirror-like surface absorbs light, whereas the brick wall reflects light in a regular way.
The brick wall reflects light in a regular way, whereas the mirror-like surface scatters light.

questions.question: What must happen for a person to see a non-luminous object like a book?
options: Light from the eye must travel to the book and illuminate it.
Light emitted or reflected from the book must enter the eye.
The book must absorb all light that strikes its surface.
The book must bend light around it so it reaches the retina.

questions.question: Through which part of the eye does light enter, and where is it detected?
options: Enters through the retina and is detected by the pupil.
Enters through the pupil and is detected by the retina.
Enters through the iris and is detected by the lens.
Enters through the pupil and is detected by the optic nerve.

questions.question: Why can a laser beam travelling through clean, dust-free air usually not be seen from the side?
options: The laser beam is moving too fast for human eyes to detect.
The light does not hit any particles to reflect or scatter it towards the eye.
The air particles absorb all of the light from the laser beam.
Clean air acts as a mirror and reflects the beam away from the eye.

questions.question: What is an echo?
options: A sound that has been absorbed by a soft surface.
A sound that is heard again after reflecting off a hard surface and travelling back.
A sound that has its frequency increased when passing through water.
A vibration that is too fast to be heard by human ears.

questions.question: Why do smooth, flat walls produce clearer echoes than highly irregular rock walls?
options: Smooth surfaces absorb all sound waves, creating silent zones.
Irregular surfaces reflect sound in many directions, spreading it out, whereas smooth surfaces help produce echoes.
Smooth surfaces increase the frequency of the sound waves.
Irregular surfaces act like mirrors and reflect all sound in a single, regular direction.

questions.question: Why do soft materials absorb sound waves effectively?
options: Sound waves transfer energy by making the particles in the soft materials vibrate.
Soft materials reflect sound waves in a single, regular direction.
The particles in soft materials are held by extremely strong forces that stop all movement.
Soft materials speed up sound waves until they are too fast to hear.

questions.question: In light reflection, what is the 'normal'?
options: A line drawn parallel to the mirror surface.
An imaginary line drawn at 90 degrees to the point of reflection.
The path that the incoming light ray takes.
The path that the reflected light ray takes.

questions.question: If a ray of light hits a flat mirror with an angle of incidence of 35 degrees, what is the angle of reflection?
options: 55 degrees, on the same side of the normal.
35 degrees, on the other side of the normal.
90 degrees, along the normal.
0 degrees, back along the path of incidence.

questions.question: If you stand 2 metres in front of a flat mirror, where does your reflection appear to be?
options: 4 metres in front of the mirror.
2 metres behind the mirror, directly opposite you.
1 metre behind the mirror, shifted to the left.
Right on the surface of the mirror.

questions.question: When you look at your reflection in a plain vertical mirror, how is the image described?
options: Upside down and laterally inverted.
Right way up but laterally inverted.
Upside down and not laterally inverted.
Right way up and not laterally inverted.

questions.question: How do transparent objects differ from opaque objects regarding light?
options: Transparent objects absorb light, whereas opaque objects transmit it.
Transparent objects transmit light, whereas opaque objects do not let light travel through them.
Transparent objects reflect light regularly, whereas opaque objects transmit it.
Transparent objects create shadows, whereas opaque objects do not.

questions.question: What is a shadow?
options: An area where light is bent around an object.
An unlit area in the shape of an object that is blocking light.
A region where light rays are reflected back to their source.
A direct image of the light source itself.

questions.question: What is amplitude, and how does it affect a sound?
options: It is the number of vibrations per second; greater amplitude makes a higher pitch.
It is a measure of the size of a vibration; greater amplitude makes a louder sound.
It is the speed of the sound wave; greater amplitude makes the sound travel faster.
It is a measure of the size of a vibration; greater amplitude makes a quieter sound.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes frequency and its effect on sound?
options: Frequency is how loud a sound is; greater frequency makes a louder sound.
Frequency measures how often vibrations occur; greater frequency makes a higher pitch.
Frequency measures the distance of a vibration; greater frequency makes a lower pitch.
Frequency is how fast a sound travels; greater frequency means it travels faster through solids.

questions.question: Why is it impossible for sound to travel through a vacuum?
options: A vacuum has too much air pressure which stops vibrations.
Sound waves are vibrations of particles, and a vacuum contains no particles.
A vacuum absorbs all sound energy and converts it into light.
Sound waves travel too fast in a vacuum to be detected.
